title: Exercise 7B · Q14
summary: Find the net North–South and East–West displacement, then apply Pythagoras.
alt: Exercise 7B · Q14: A courier travels due North at an average speed of 40 km/h for 6 minutes to collect a parcel, before travelling 10 km due East to deliver it. He then travels due South at an average speed of 30 km/h for 12 minutes to collect another parcel. Find the shortest distance between the courier and his starting point.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: A courier travels **North** at **40 km/h** for **6 min** (**O→A**), then **10 km East** to deliver a parcel (**A→B**), then **South** at **30 km/h** for **12 min** to collect another parcel (**B→C**). Find the shortest distance between the courier (at **C**) and the starting point **O**.

steps.title: Net North–South displacement
steps.narration: North leg = 40 × 6/60 = **4 km**. South leg = 30 × 12/60 = **6 km**. Net displacement from **O**:\[\begin{aligned}\text{South} &: 6 - 4 = \role{legB}{2}\ \text{km}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Spot the right angle
steps.narration: In the right angle between East and South, the right angle is at **A**. The **hypotenuse** is the side opposite the right angle — the longest side. East and South are perpendicular directions.

steps.title: Pythagoras' theorem
steps.narration: **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{\text{hypotenuse}^2} &= \role{legA}{\text{leg}^2} + \role{legB}{\text{leg}^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 104 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{\text{hypotenuse}^2} &= \role{legA}{\text{leg}^2} + \role{legB}{\text{leg}^2} \\ \role{hyp}{OC^2} &= \role{legA}{10^2} + \role{legB}{2^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{100} + \role{legB}{4} \\ &= \role{hyp}{104} \\ \role{hyp}{OC} &= \sqrt{104} = \role{ans}{10.2\ \text{km}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Check the net South
challenges.prompt: North leg = 4 km, South leg = 6 km. What is the net South displacement from the start?
challenges.hint: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

takeaways: Track the **net** North–South and East–West movement; the straight-line distance uses only those totals.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Grid tip
notes.text: Put the start at the origin. North/South and East/West are always perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies to the two net displacements.
